text: Welcome to Week 12. This lecture is about what happens when systems are pushed beyond their normal comfort zone, how we test them, and how we keep enough observability to understand failures when they happen. The big theme across the week is that stress is not just a bigger version of normal traffic. It changes system behavior, exposes bottlenecks, and forces us to think carefully about evidence, capacity, and control.

The key idea here is that system stress starts when load exceeds what the system can comfortably handle. That extra load can saturate resources, which then raises latency, and once latency rises far enough, errors begin to appear. This sequence matters because it reminds us that failures are often gradual, not sudden. An engineer should be looking for the chain from pressure to saturation to delay to visible failure, because that is usually where the real design problem lives.

When a system is under stress, the first clues usually come from resource signals. High CPU usage can tell you the service is busy, memory pressure can hint at growth or leaks, disk queueing can mean storage is the bottleneck, and network congestion can slow everything down. These signals matter because they are often the earliest measurable evidence that latency is about to worsen. A common mistake is waiting for user complaints instead of watching these indicators proactively.

Load testing should be treated like a process, not a one-off experiment. First you define the scenario, then you generate the load, measure the system, analyze the results, and finally tune the design or configuration. The important discipline here is that testing is only useful if it is tied to a clear question. Imagine you are defending a system in front of a reviewer: you need to explain what workload you used, what evidence you collected, and what changed after analysis.

Different traffic patterns reveal different weaknesses. A ramp-up test lets you see when performance starts to degrade as load grows gradually. A spike test checks how the system reacts to a sudden burst. A soak test looks for problems that only appear after sustained pressure, like memory leaks or resource exhaustion. A step test helps you compare behavior across discrete load levels. The main idea is that the shape of the workload matters as much as the size.

Under stress, observability has to give you three things: signals, context, and causality. Metrics tell you that something is changing, logs tell you what happened in detail, and traces help you follow the request path so you can understand where delay was introduced. Alerts then pull those pieces together into something actionable. This matters because stressed systems often fail in ways that are hard to infer from a single data source. Good observability lets you explain the failure instead of guessing.

Here is the uncomfortable failure pattern to keep in mind: once the app is overloaded, requests start piling up in a queue, then they wait too long and time out, and those timeouts trigger retries. The retries add even more load, which pushes the system further into distress. This is the classic positive feedback loop that hides behind a happy-path benchmark. The evidence students should capture here is the sequence of queue growth, timeout behavior, and retry amplification, because that is what proves the failure mechanism.

The protected property here is system stability under pressure. Caching reduces repeated work, backpressure controls how much demand enters the system, autoscaling adds capacity when possible, and circuit breakers stop a failing dependency from dragging everything down. None of these is free. Each one introduces trade-offs in consistency, complexity, cost, or user experience. The engineering judgment question is not whether a control exists, but whether it protects the right property at an acceptable price.

Before you run a stress test, define the workload clearly so you know what you are trying to learn. During the test, measure latency, throughput, and error rate, and watch CPU, memory, disk, and network closely. Afterward, compare what you expected with what actually happened, then use logs and traces to explain the root cause. The goal is not just to find a failure, but to turn that failure into a defensible design improvement, whether that means more capacity, better controls, or both.
